### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s1 | A quantity shrinks by 2% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 0.98 | hint: Taking away 2% of an amount $A$ leaves $A - 0.02A$. Factor out $A$. | [A - 0.02A = A(1 - 0.02)] 2% is $0.02$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 0.98] Every year the amount is multiplied by 0.98, a number less than 1, which is decay.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s2 | A quantity grows by 6% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 1.06 | hint: Adding 6% of an amount $A$ leaves $A + 0.06A$. Factor out $A$. | [A + 0.06A = A(1 + 0.06)] 6% is $0.06$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 1.06] Every year the amount is multiplied by 1.06.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s4 | A town's population after $t$ years is $f(t) = 250(1.06)^{t}$. By what percent does it grow each year? Give just the number, like 5 for 5%. => 6 | hint: The growth factor is $1 + r$ for growth and $1 - r$ for decay, with $r$ as a decimal. | [1.06 = 1 + 0.06] The factor 1.06 is more than 1, so this is growth. || [0.06 = 6\%] Each year it gains 6% of what it had.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s5 | A quantity grows by 25% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 1.25 | hint: Adding 25% of an amount $A$ leaves $A + 0.25A$. Factor out $A$. | [A + 0.25A = A(1 + 0.25)] 25% is $0.25$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 1.25] Every year the amount is multiplied by 1.25.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s6 | Evaluate $2 \cdot 2^{x}$ when $x = -2$. Give an exact answer. => 1/2 | hint: A negative exponent means a reciprocal: $2^{-2} = \frac{1}{2^{2}}$. | [2 \cdot 2^{-2} = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{2^{2}}] $b^{-n} = \frac{1}{b^n}$ because $b^{-n} \cdot b^n = b^0 = 1$ (Algebra 1 Unit 6). || [= \frac{2}{4} = \frac{1}{2}] Going left on the graph, the values shrink toward 0 but stay positive.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s7 | Evaluate $5 \cdot 2^{x}$ when $x = 4$. => 80 | hint: Exponent first: work out $2^{4}$, then multiply by 5. Only the 2 is raised to the power. | [5 \cdot 2^{4}] Substitute. || [5 \cdot 16] $2^{4}$ is 4 factors of 2. || [80] Not $(5 \cdot 2)^{4}$: the exponent belongs to the base $2$ alone.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s12 | Evaluate $40\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$ when $x = 3$. => 5 | hint: $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = \frac{1}{2^{3}}$. Each step of 1 in $x$ divides by 2. | [40\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = 40 \cdot \frac{1}{8}] A power of a fraction is the power of the top over the power of the bottom. || [\frac{40}{8} = 5] The starting value 40 was divided by 2, 3 times over.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s115 | Evaluate $128\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{x}$ when $x = 3$. => 2 | hint: $\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3} = \frac{1}{4^{3}}$. Each step of 1 in $x$ divides by 4. | [128\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{3} = 128 \cdot \frac{1}{64}] A power of a fraction is the power of the top over the power of the bottom. || [\frac{128}{64} = 2] The starting value 128 was divided by 4, 3 times over.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s116 | A town's population after $t$ years is $f(t) = 5000(1.3)^{t}$. By what percent does it grow each year? Give just the number, like 5 for 5%. => 30 | hint: The growth factor is $1 + r$ for growth and $1 - r$ for decay, with $r$ as a decimal. | [1.3 = 1 + 0.3] The factor 1.3 is more than 1, so this is growth. || [0.3 = 30\%] Each year it gains 30% of what it had.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s122 | A quantity shrinks by 8% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 0.92 | hint: Taking away 8% of an amount $A$ leaves $A - 0.08A$. Factor out $A$. | [A - 0.08A = A(1 - 0.08)] 8% is $0.08$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 0.92] Every year the amount is multiplied by 0.92, a number less than 1, which is decay.

The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 1.12] Every year the amount is multiplied by 1.12.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s172 | Evaluate $4 \cdot 2^{x}$ when $x = 4$. => 64 | hint: Exponent first: work out $2^{4}$, then multiply by 4. Only the 2 is raised to the power. | [4 \cdot 2^{4}] Substitute. || [4 \cdot 16] $2^{4}$ is 4 factors of 2. || [64] Not $(4 \cdot 2)^{4}$: the exponent belongs to the base $2$ alone.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s174 | A quantity shrinks by 20% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 0.8 | hint: Taking away 20% of an amount $A$ leaves $A - 0.2A$. Factor out $A$. | [A - 0.2A = A(1 - 0.2)] 20% is $0.2$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 0.8] Every year the amount is multiplied by 0.8, a number less than 1, which is decay.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s230 | Evaluate $16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$ when $x = 4$. => 1 | hint: $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4} = \frac{1}{2^{4}}$. Each step of 1 in $x$ divides by 2. | [16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4} = 16 \cdot \frac{1}{16}] A power of a fraction is the power of the top over the power of the bottom. || [\frac{16}{16} = 1] The starting value 16 was divided by 2, 4 times over.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s231 | A car's value, in dollars, after $t$ years is $f(t) = 5000(0.96)^{t}$. By what percent does it shrink each year? Give just the number, like 5 for 5%. => 4 | hint: The growth factor is $1 + r$ for growth and $1 - r$ for decay, with $r$ as a decimal. | [0.96 = 1 - 0.04] The factor 0.96 is less than 1, so this is decay. || [0.04 = 4\%] Each year it loses 4% of what it had.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s237 | A quantity grows by 6% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 1.06 | hint: Adding 6% of an amount $A$ leaves $A + 0.06A$. Factor out $A$. | [A + 0.06A = A(1 + 0.06)] 6% is $0.06$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 1.06] Every year the amount is multiplied by 1.06.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s286 | A town's population after $t$ years is $f(t) = 1200(1.1)^{t}$. By what percent does it grow each year? Give just the number, like 5 for 5%. => 10 | hint: The growth factor is $1 + r$ for growth and $1 - r$ for decay, with $r$ as a decimal. | [1.1 = 1 + 0.1] The factor 1.1 is more than 1, so this is growth. || [0.1 = 10\%] Each year it gains 10% of what it had.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s287 | A quantity grows by 12% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 1.12 | hint: Adding 12% of an amount $A$ leaves $A + 0.12A$. Factor out $A$. | [A + 0.12A = A(1 + 0.12)] 12% is $0.12$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 1.12] Every year the amount is multiplied by 1.12.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s288 | A quantity shrinks by 40% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 0.6 | hint: Taking away 40% of an amount $A$ leaves $A - 0.4A$. Factor out $A$. | [A - 0.4A = A(1 - 0.4)] 40% is $0.4$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 0.6] Every year the amount is multiplied by 0.6, a number less than 1, which is decay.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s398 | A car's value, in dollars, after $t$ years is $f(t) = 1200(0.9)^{t}$. By what percent does it shrink each year? Give just the number, like 5 for 5%. => 10 | hint: The growth factor is $1 + r$ for growth and $1 - r$ for decay, with $r$ as a decimal. | [0.9 = 1 - 0.1] The factor 0.9 is less than 1, so this is decay. || [0.1 = 10\%] Each year it loses 10% of what it had.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s399 | Evaluate $16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}$ when $x = 4$. => 1 | hint: $\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4} = \frac{1}{2^{4}}$. Each step of 1 in $x$ divides by 2. | [16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{4} = 16 \cdot \frac{1}{16}] A power of a fraction is the power of the top over the power of the bottom. || [\frac{16}{16} = 1] The starting value 16 was divided by 2, 4 times over.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#0 s400 | A quantity grows by 10% each year, so each year it is multiplied by the same growth factor $b$. Find $b$ as a decimal. => 1.1 | hint: Adding 10% of an amount $A$ leaves $A + 0.1A$. Factor out $A$. | [A + 0.1A = A(1 + 0.1)] 10% is $0.1$. The distributive property, run backwards. || [b = 1.1] Every year the amount is multiplied by 1.1.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s1 | A radioactive sample of 48 grams decays to 3 grams in 120 years. What is its half-life, in years? => 30 | hint: How many times must 48 be halved to reach 3? Those halvings took 120 years. | [\frac{3}{48} = \frac{1}{16} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{4}] The mass was multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ a total of 4 times. || [4 \text{ half-lives} = 120 \text{ years}]  || [h = \frac{120}{4} = 30] Check: $48\left(\frac12\right)^{120/30} = 48\left(\frac12\right)^{4} = 3$.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s6 | A radioactive sample has a mass of 48 grams and a half-life of 5 days. How many grams are left after 20 days? => 3 | hint: How many half-lives fit into 20 days? ### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s7 | A culture starts with 50 bacteria and doubles every 8 days. How many bacteria are there after 32 days? => 800 | hint: How many doublings fit into 32 days? | [N = 50 \cdot 2^{t/8}] The exponent $\frac{t}{8}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [N = 50 \cdot 2^{32/8} = 50 \cdot 2^{4}] 32 days is 4 doubling periods. || [N = 50 \cdot 16 = 800]

Do that 2 times. | [V(t) = 5000(1.04)^{t}] Gaining 4% means multiplying by $1 + 0.04 = 1.04$. || [V(2) = 5000(1.04)^{2} = 5000(1.0816)] 2 years, 2 multiplications. || [V(2) = 5408] 
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s49 | A culture starts with 300 bacteria and doubles every 6 days. After how many days are there 1200 bacteria? => 12 | hint: Divide 1200 by 300 to see the total growth factor. How many doublings make that factor? | [N = 300 \cdot 2^{t/6}] The exponent $\frac{t}{6}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [300 \cdot 2^{t/6} = 1200 \;\Rightarrow\; 2^{t/6} = 4] Divide both sides by 300. || [2^{t/6} = 2^{2} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{t}{6} = 2] $4 = 2^{2}$: that's 2 doublings. || [t = 12] 2 periods of 6 days.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s50 | A radioactive sample has a mass of 24 grams and a half-life of 4 hours. How many grams are left after 12 hours? => 3 | hint: How many half-lives fit into 12 hours? Each one halves the mass. | [A = 24\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/4}] The exponent $\frac{t}{4}$ counts half-lives. || [A = 24\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = \frac{24}{8}] 12 hours is 3 half-lives. || [A = 3] Halving 3 times: 24, 12, 6, 3.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s51 | A culture starts with 50 bacteria and doubles every 4 hours. How many bacteria are there after 8 hours? => 200 | hint: How many doublings fit into 8 hours? | [N = 50 \cdot 2^{t/4}] The exponent $\frac{t}{4}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [N = 50 \cdot 2^{8/4} = 50 \cdot 2^{2}] 8 hours is 2 doubling periods. || [N = 50 \cdot 4 = 200] 
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s52 | A culture starts with 50 bacteria and doubles every 4 days. After how many days are there 1600 bacteria? => 20 | hint: Divide 1600 by 50 to see the total growth factor. How many doublings make that factor? | [N = 50 \cdot 2^{t/4}] The exponent $\frac{t}{4}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [50 \cdot 2^{t/4} = 1600 \;\Rightarrow\; 2^{t/4} = 32] Divide both sides by 50. || [2^{t/4} = 2^{5} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{t}{4} = 5] $32 = 2^{5}$: that's 5 doublings. || [t = 20] 5 periods of 4 days.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s56 | A culture starts with 200 bacteria and doubles every 6 hours. How many bacteria are there after 18 hours? => 1600 | hint: How many doublings fit into 18 hours? | [N = 200 \cdot 2^{t/6}] The exponent $\frac{t}{6}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [N = 200 \cdot 2^{18/6} = 200 \cdot 2^{3}] 18 hours is 3 doubling periods. || [N = 200 \cdot 8 = 1600] 
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s57 | A radioactive sample of 20 grams decays to 5 grams in 24 days. What is its half-life, in days? => 12 | hint: How many times must 20 be halved to reach 5? Those halvings took 24 days. | [\frac{5}{20} = \frac{1}{4} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}] The mass was multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ a total of 2 times. || [2 \text{ half-lives} = 24 \text{ days}]  || [h = \frac{24}{2} = 12] Check: $20\left(\frac12\right)^{24/12} = 20\left(\frac12\right)^{2} = 5$.

Those halvings took 16 hours. | [\frac{5}{20} = \frac{1}{4} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}] The mass was multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ a total of 2 times. || [2 \text{ half-lives} = 16 \text{ hours}]  || [h = \frac{16}{2} = 8] Check: $20\left(\frac12\right)^{16/8} = 20\left(\frac12\right)^{2} = 5$.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s64 | A car is worth 4000 dollars, and it loses 15% of its value each year. What is it worth after 2 years, in dollars? => 2890 | hint: Each year multiplies the value by $0.85$. Do that 2 times. | [V(t) = 4000(0.85)^{t}] Losing 15% means multiplying by $1 - 0.15 = 0.85$. || [V(2) = 4000(0.85)^{2} = 4000(0.7225)] 2 years, 2 multiplications. || [V(2) = 2890] Not $4000 - 2 \cdot 600$: each year's 15% is taken from a smaller value.

### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s69 | A radioactive sample of 192 grams decays to 6 grams in 100 years. What is its half-life, in years? => 20 | hint: How many times must 192 be halved to reach 6? Do that 2 times. | [V(t) = 5000(0.98)^{t}] Losing 2% means multiplying by $1 - 0.02 = 0.98$. || [V(2) = 5000(0.98)^{2} = 5000(0.9604)] 2 years, 2 multiplications. || [V(2) = 4802] Not $5000 - 2 \cdot 100$: each year's 2% is taken from a smaller value.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s199 | A car is worth 5000 dollars, and it loses 15% of its value each year. What is it worth after 2 years, in dollars? => 3612.5 | hint: Each year multiplies the value by $0.85$. Do that 2 times. | [V(t) = 5000(0.85)^{t}] Losing 15% means multiplying by $1 - 0.15 = 0.85$. || [V(2) = 5000(0.85)^{2} = 5000(0.7225)] 2 years, 2 multiplications. || [V(2) = 3612.5] Not $5000 - 2 \cdot 750$: each year's 15% is taken from a smaller value.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s200 | A culture starts with 300 bacteria and doubles every 4 days. After how many days are there 4800 bacteria? => 16 | hint: Divide 4800 by 300 to see the total growth factor. How many doublings make that factor? | [N = 300 \cdot 2^{t/4}] The exponent $\frac{t}{4}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [300 \cdot 2^{t/4} = 4800 \;\Rightarrow\; 2^{t/4} = 16] Divide both sides by 300. || [2^{t/4} = 2^{4} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{t}{4} = 4] $16 = 2^{4}$: that's 4 doublings. || [t = 16] 4 periods of 4 days.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s201 | A radioactive sample has a mass of 80 grams and a half-life of 20 hours. How many grams are left after 60 hours? => 10 | hint: How many half-lives fit into 60 hours? Each one halves the mass. | [A = 80\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/20}] The exponent $\frac{t}{20}$ counts half-lives. || [A = 80\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3} = \frac{80}{8}] 60 hours is 3 half-lives. || [A = 10] Halving 3 times: 80, 40, 20, 10.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s202 | A culture starts with 500 bacteria and doubles every 3 hours. How many bacteria are there after 9 hours? => 4000 | hint: How many doublings fit into 9 hours? | [N = 500 \cdot 2^{t/3}] The exponent $\frac{t}{3}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [N = 500 \cdot 2^{9/3} = 500 \cdot 2^{3}] 9 hours is 3 doubling periods. || [N = 500 \cdot 8 = 4000] 
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s203 | A radioactive sample of 40 grams decays to 5 grams in 12 years. What is its half-life, in years? => 4 | hint: How many times must 40 be halved to reach 5? Those halvings took 12 years. | [\frac{5}{40} = \frac{1}{8} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{3}] The mass was multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ a total of 3 times. || [3 \text{ half-lives} = 12 \text{ years}]  || [h = \frac{12}{3} = 4] Check: $40\left(\frac12\right)^{12/4} = 40\left(\frac12\right)^{3} = 5$.

How many doublings make that factor? | [N = 100 \cdot 2^{t/4}] The exponent $\frac{t}{4}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [100 \cdot 2^{t/4} = 1600 \;\Rightarrow\; 2^{t/4} = 16] Divide both sides by 100. || [2^{t/4} = 2^{4} \;\Rightarrow\; \frac{t}{4} = 4] $16 = 2^{4}$: that's 4 doublings. || [t = 16] 4 periods of 4 hours.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s298 | A radioactive sample has a mass of 40 grams and a half-life of 12 years. How many grams are left after 24 years? => 10 | hint: How many half-lives fit into 24 years? Each one halves the mass. | [A = 40\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/12}] The exponent $\frac{t}{12}$ counts half-lives. || [A = 40\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2} = \frac{40}{4}] 24 years is 2 half-lives. || [A = 10] Halving 2 times: 40, 20, 10.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s299 | A radioactive sample of 60 grams decays to 15 grams in 24 hours. What is its half-life, in hours? => 12 | hint: How many times must 60 be halved to reach 15? Those halvings took 24 hours. | [\frac{15}{60} = \frac{1}{4} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}] The mass was multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ a total of 2 times. || [2 \text{ half-lives} = 24 \text{ hours}]  || [h = \frac{24}{2} = 12] Check: $60\left(\frac12\right)^{24/12} = 60\left(\frac12\right)^{2} = 15$.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s300 | A painting is worth 1000 dollars, and its value grows by 20% each year. What is it worth after 3 years, in dollars? => 1728 | hint: Each year multiplies the value by $1.2$. Do that 3 times. | [V(t) = 1000(1.2)^{t}] Gaining 20% means multiplying by $1 + 0.2 = 1.2$. || [V(3) = 1000(1.2)^{3} = 1000(1.728)] 3 years, 3 multiplications. || [V(3) = 1728] 
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s301 | A radioactive sample has a mass of 160 grams and a half-life of 30 days. How many grams are left after 150 days? => 5 | hint: How many half-lives fit into 150 days? Each one halves the mass. | [A = 160\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t/30}] The exponent $\frac{t}{30}$ counts half-lives. || [A = 160\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{5} = \frac{160}{32}] 150 days is 5 half-lives. || [A = 5] Halving 5 times: 160, 80, 40, 20, 10, 5.

How many bacteria are there after 12 days? => 3200 | hint: How many doublings fit into 12 days? | [N = 200 \cdot 2^{t/3}] The exponent $\frac{t}{3}$ counts how many doubling periods have passed. || [N = 200 \cdot 2^{12/3} = 200 \cdot 2^{4}] 12 days is 4 doubling periods. || [N = 200 \cdot 16 = 3200] 
### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s398 | A painting is worth 5000 dollars, and its value grows by 20% each year. What is it worth after 2 years, in dollars? => 7200 | hint: Each year multiplies the value by $1.2$. Do that 2 times. | [V(t) = 5000(1.2)^{t}] Gaining 20% means multiplying by $1 + 0.2 = 1.2$. || [V(2) = 5000(1.2)^{2} = 5000(1.44)] 2 years, 2 multiplications. || [V(2) = 7200]

### exponential-growth-and-decay#1 s400 | A radioactive sample of 40 grams decays to 10 grams in 20 years. What is its half-life, in years? => 10 | hint: How many times must 40 be halved to reach 10? Those halvings took 20 years. | [\frac{10}{40} = \frac{1}{4} = \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{2}] The mass was multiplied by $\frac{1}{2}$ a total of 2 times. || [2 \text{ half-lives} = 20 \text{ years}]  || [h = \frac{20}{2} = 10] Check: $40\left(\frac12\right)^{20/10} = 40\left(\frac12\right)^{2} = 10$.
### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s1 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 24)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (3, 2) | hint: Write both equations and divide one by the other. The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 6, \quad ab^{3} = 24] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{24}{6} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 4] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 2] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{6}{2} = 3] From the first equation, $a \cdot 2 = 6$. || [y = 3 \cdot 2^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $3 \cdot 2^{3} = 24$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

(Decay, since $b < 1$.)

Then use the other point to find $b$. | [a \cdot b^0 = 8 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 8] At $x = 0$, $b^0 = 1$, so the $y$-intercept is $a$ itself. || [8 \cdot b = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; b = \frac{1}{4}] Substitute the second point and divide by 8. || [y = 8 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{x}] Check: at $x = 1$, $8 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1} = 2$. (Decay, since $b < 1$.)

### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s32 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 54)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (2, 3) | hint: Write both equations and divide one by the other. The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 6, \quad ab^{3} = 54] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{54}{6} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 9] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 3] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{6}{3} = 2] From the first equation, $a \cdot 3 = 6$. || [y = 2 \cdot 3^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $2 \cdot 3^{3} = 54$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

Then use the other point to find $b$. | [a \cdot b^0 = 4 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 4] At $x = 0$, $b^0 = 1$, so the $y$-intercept is $a$ itself. || [4 \cdot b = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; b = \frac{1}{2}] Substitute the second point and divide by 4. || [y = 4 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}] Check: at $x = 1$, $4 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{1} = 2$. (Decay, since $b < 1$.)

### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s68 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 8)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (1, 2) | hint: Write both equations and divide one by the other. The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 2, \quad ab^{3} = 8] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{8}{2} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 4] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 2] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{2}{2} = 1] From the first equation, $a \cdot 2 = 2$. || [y = 1 \cdot 2^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $1 \cdot 2^{3} = 8$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

Then use the other point to find $b$. | [a \cdot b^0 = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 6] At $x = 0$, $b^0 = 1$, so the $y$-intercept is $a$ itself. || [6 \cdot b^{2} = 24 \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 4] Substitute the second point and divide by 6. || [b = 2] $2^{2} = 4$, and $b$ must be positive. || [y = 6 \cdot 2^{x}] Check: at $x = 2$, $6 \cdot 2^{2} = 24$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)
### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s95 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 54)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (2, 3) | hint: Write both equations and divide one by the other. The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 6, \quad ab^{3} = 54] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{54}{6} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 9] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 3] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{6}{3} = 2] From the first equation, $a \cdot 3 = 6$. || [y = 2 \cdot 3^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $2 \cdot 3^{3} = 54$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 6, \quad ab^{3} = 54] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{54}{6} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 9] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 3] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{6}{3} = 2] From the first equation, $a \cdot 3 = 6$. || [y = 2 \cdot 3^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $2 \cdot 3^{3} = 54$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)
### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s127 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(0, 6)$ and $(2, 150)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (6, 5) | hint: At $x = 0$ the power is 1, so $y = a$. Then use the other point to find $b$. | [a \cdot b^0 = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 6] At $x = 0$, $b^0 = 1$, so the $y$-intercept is $a$ itself. || [6 \cdot b^{2} = 150 \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 25] Substitute the second point and divide by 6. || [b = 5] $5^{2} = 25$, and $b$ must be positive. || [y = 6 \cdot 5^{x}] Check: at $x = 2$, $6 \cdot 5^{2} = 150$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

Then use the other point to find $b$. | [a \cdot b^0 = 6 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 6] At $x = 0$, $b^0 = 1$, so the $y$-intercept is $a$ itself. || [6 \cdot b^{2} = 24 \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 4] Substitute the second point and divide by 6. || [b = 2] $2^{2} = 4$, and $b$ must be positive. || [y = 6 \cdot 2^{x}] Check: at $x = 2$, $6 \cdot 2^{2} = 24$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

(Growth, since $b > 1$.)
### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s160 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(0, 24)$ and $(2, 6)$. Find $a$ and $b$. (Decay, since $b < 1$.)

### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s163 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(1, 6)$ and $(3, 54)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (2, 3) | hint: Write both equations and divide one by the other. The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 6, \quad ab^{3} = 54] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{54}{6} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 9] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 3] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{6}{3} = 2] From the first equation, $a \cdot 3 = 6$. || [y = 2 \cdot 3^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $2 \cdot 3^{3} = 54$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)

The $a$'s cancel. | [ab = 6, \quad ab^{3} = 24] Each point satisfies $y = ab^x$. || [\frac{ab^{3}}{ab} = \frac{24}{6} \;\Rightarrow\; b^{2} = 4] Divide the equations: $a$ cancels, and $\frac{b^{3}}{b^{1}} = b^{2}$. || [b = 2] $b$ must be positive. || [a = \frac{6}{2} = 3] From the first equation, $a \cdot 2 = 6$. || [y = 3 \cdot 2^{x}] Check: at $x = 3$, $3 \cdot 2^{3} = 24$. (Growth, since $b > 1$.)
### exponential-growth-and-decay#2 s254 | The graph of $y = a \cdot b^{x}$ (with $b > 0$) passes through $(0, 8)$ and $(1, 2)$. Find $a$ and $b$. Give them as $(a, b)$. => (8, 1/4) | hint: At $x = 0$ the power is 1, so $y = a$. Then use the other point to find $b$. | [a \cdot b^0 = 8 \;\Rightarrow\; a = 8] At $x = 0$, $b^0 = 1$, so the $y$-intercept is $a$ itself. || [8 \cdot b = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; b = \frac{1}{4}] Substitute the second point and divide by 8. || [y = 8 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{x}] Check: at $x = 1$, $8 \cdot \left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^{1} = 2$. (Decay, since $b < 1$.)

### logarithms-as-inverse-exponents#0 s6 | Evaluate $\log\nolimits_{8} 4$. Give an exact answer. => 2/3 | hint: Write 8 and 4 as powers of the same number, 2. | [8^{x} = 4] The question the logarithm asks. || [(2^{3})^{x} = 2^{2} \;\Rightarrow\; 2^{3x} = 2^{2}] $8 = 2^{3}$ and $4 = 2^{2}$. Power rule on the left. || [3x = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{2}{3}] Equal powers of 2 have equal exponents, because $2^{x}$ is one-to-one.

Power rule on the left. || [3x = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; x = \frac{1}{3}] Equal powers of 2 have equal exponents, because $2^{x}$ is one-to-one.

In general $f^{-1}(x) = \log_{3}(x - 3)$.

### logarithms-as-inverse-exponents#2 s251 | Let $f(x) = 5^{x} + 4$. Find $f^{-1}(29)$. => 2 | hint: $f^{-1}(29)$ is the input that $f$ sends to 29. In general $f^{-1}(x) = \log_{5}(x - 4)$.

### properties-of-logarithms#0 s399 | Evaluate $\log\nolimits_{3} 63 - \log\nolimits_{3} 7$. => 2 | hint: Quotient rule: $\log_b M - \log_b N = \log_b \frac{M}{N}$. | [\log\nolimits_{3} 63 - \log\nolimits_{3} 7 = \log\nolimits_{3} \frac{63}{7}] A difference of logs is the log of the quotient. || [= \log\nolimits_{3} 9 = 2] $9 = 3^{2}$.
### properties-of-logarithms#0 s400 | Evaluate $\frac{\log 27}{\log 3}$. Give an exact answer. => 3 | hint: Write both numbers as powers of 3, then use the power rule on the top and the bottom. | [\frac{\log 3^{3}}{\log 3^{1}} = \frac{3\log 3}{1\log 3}] Power rule, top and bottom. || [= 3] $\log 3$ cancels. By change of base, this is also $\log_{3} 27$.
### properties-of-logarithms#1 s1 | Write $\ln \frac{x^{5}}{e^{4}}$ in the form $p + q\ln x$, for $x > 0$. Give $(p, q)$. => (-4, 5) | hint: $\ln e^{4} = 4$, and the power rule handles $x^{5}$. | [\ln x^{5} - \ln e^{4}] Quotient rule. || [5\ln x - 4] $\ln e^{4} = 4$ and $\ln x^{5} = 5\ln x$. || [(p, q) = (-4, 5)]
